```{r setup, include = FALSE}
college <- read_rds("college.rds") %>%

```

## Introduction

The purpose of this project is to investigate whether there is a relationship between a college’s graduation rate and the average salary paid to its faculty. Using the U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard dataset, which includes information on thousands of institutions across the country, I focused on two continuous variables: graduation rate (GRAD_RATE) as the response variable and average faculty salary (AVGFACSAL) as the explanatory variable. I chose this question because faculty salaries can reflect how much a college invests in teaching quality and resources, and it is reasonable to wonder whether better paid instructors contribute to higher student success. To answer this question, I used exploratory visualizations, summary statistics, and a linear regression model to evaluate the strength and direction of this relationship. Because both variables are continuous, I will be using modeling to analyze the connection between faculty salary and graduation rates.


## Preprocessing

The College Scorecard dataset is large and mostly clean, but some preparation is needed before analysis. Since my research question focuses on whether graduation rate is related to average faculty salary, the first step was to extract only the columns necessary for this study. I selected C150_4 (graduation rate), AVGFACSAL (average faculty salary), and LOCALE (the location type of the institution) and stored them in a smaller dataset to work with more efficiently. Next, I renamed the variables to more fitting names so they are easier to understand during visualization and modeling. I also re-coded the LOCALE variable because it was stored as numbers that represent different geographic categories. Along with that, I did not remove missing values at this stage since row filtering is meant to occur later for the regression model.


```{r}
#Selects the columns I need for my analysis
college_reduced <- college %>%
  select(C150_4, AVGFACSAL, LOCALE)

#Renames them to the variable names I want to use
college_clean <- college_reduced %>%
  rename(
    GRAD_RATE = C150_4,
    AVGFACSAL = AVGFACSAL
  )

#Converts graduation rate from a proportion to a percentage
college_clean <- college_clean %>%
  mutate(
    GRAD_RATE = GRAD_RATE * 100
  )

#Re-codes LOCALE values so numbers are readable categories
college_clean <- college_clean %>%
  mutate(
    LOCALE = ifelse(LOCALE == -3, NA, LOCALE)
  )
 #-3 represents a missing category and converts it to NA

#Readable categories
college_clean <- college_clean %>%
  mutate(
    LOCALE = recode(
      LOCALE,
      `11` = "City: Large",
      `12` = "City: Midsize",
      `13` = "City: Small",
      `21` = "Suburb: Large",
      `22` = "Suburb: Midsize",
      `23` = "Suburb: Small",
      `31` = "Town: Outskirts",
      `32` = "Town: Distant",
      `33` = "Town: Remote",
      `41` = "Rural: Outskirts",
      `42` = "Rural: Distant",
      `43` = "Rural: Remote"
    )
  )


```


## Visualization

To begin exploring the relationship between faculty salary and graduation rate, I created many visualizations to observe variation within each variable and any variations between them. These graphs help reveal general patterns, distributions, and whether a potential relationship exists worth modeling.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Histogram of college graduation rates

ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "pink", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Graduation Rates",
    x = "Graduation Rate Percentage",
    y = "Count of Colleges"
  )

```

This histogram shows that graduation rates vary widely among colleges. Most schools fall between 30% and 70%, with fewer institutions having extremely low or extremely high rates. The distribution is slightly right-skewed, meaning more schools have moderate graduation rates rather than very high ones. This spread suggests that many factors impact graduation rates, which makes it relevant to examine whether faculty salary plays a role.



```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Histogram of faculty salary distribution

ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = AVGFACSAL)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000, fill = "purple", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Average Faculty Salaries",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (US Dollars)",
    y = "Count of Colleges"
  )

```

This graph shows that most colleges pay faculty between $40,000 and $80,000, with fewer institutions offering very high salaries. The distribution is slightly right-skewed, meaning high-salary colleges are less common. The wide spread in salary suggests that institutions noticeably differ in funding and resources, which may contribute to differences in graduation outcomes.


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Scatter plot showing association between salary and graduation rate

ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = AVGFACSAL, y = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Graduation Rate vs. Average Faculty Salary",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (US Dollars)",
    y = "Graduation Rate Percentage"
  )

```

The scatter plot shows a positive trend, meaning colleges with higher faculty salaries tend to have higher graduation rates. However, the points are fairly spread out, suggesting salary alone doesn't fully predict graduation success. This indicates that salary may influence outcomes but is only one of several contributing factors.


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Facet plot to compare relationship across different campus locales
college_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(LOCALE)) %>%  # Prevent NA panel from appearing
  ggplot(aes(x = AVGFACSAL, y = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "pink") +
  facet_wrap(~ LOCALE) +
  labs(
    title = "Graduation Rate vs Salary by Locale",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (USD)",
    y = "Graduation Rate (%)"
  )

```

When evaluated by locale, the trend between salary and graduation appears in most settings, but the strength varies. Urban and suburban colleges tend to show slightly closer clustering and higher salaries, while rural schools show more spread and lower average graduation rates. This suggests location could be a factor that interacts with salary, meaning differences in resources across locales could influence student outcomes.



## Summary Statistics

In this section I find summary statistics for the main variables in my analysis. Graduation rate (GRAD_RATE) and average faculty salary (AVGFACSAL) are both continuous variables, and locale is a categorical variable that describes the setting of each institution, like the city, suburb, town, or rural area. Looking at summary statistics helps establish and confirm the patterns seen in the plots and provides numerical context for the later modeling.

```{r}
#Count the number of schools in each locale category
college_clean %>%
  group_by(LOCALE) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  head()   

```

This table shows how many colleges fall into each locale category. Some groups have more institutions than others, meaning that certain campus environments, like large cities and suburbs, are more common in the dataset. Because of this variation, some locale types will influence results more than others, so it is important to keep representation in mind when comparing outcomes across groups.


```{r}
#Summary statistics for graduation rate by locale
grad_stats <- college_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(GRAD_RATE)) %>%      
  filter(!is.na(LOCALE)) %>% #only for summary purposes         
  group_by(LOCALE) %>%
  summarize(
    n         = n(),
    mean_grad = mean(GRAD_RATE),
    median_grad = median(GRAD_RATE),
    min_grad  = min(GRAD_RATE),
    max_grad  = max(GRAD_RATE),
    sd_grad   = sd(GRAD_RATE),
    iqr_grad  = IQR(GRAD_RATE)
  )
```

These statistics describe how graduation rates vary based on college locale. The mean and median help show the average graduation rate for each group, while the minimum and maximum reveal the range of outcomes. The standard deviation and IQR show how spread out the graduation rates are within each type of institution. Missing GRAD_RATE values caused warnings originally, so I temporarily filtered rows for the summary table only, but kept the full dataset together for later modeling.


```{r}
#Summary statistics for average faculty salary by locale
salary_stats <- college_clean %>%
  group_by(LOCALE) %>%
  summarize(
    n            = sum(!is.na(AVGFACSAL)),
    mean_salary   = mean(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_salary = median(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_salary    = min(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_salary    = max(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_salary     = sd(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_salary    = IQR(AVGFACSAL, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

This table summarizes average faculty salary across different locales. The mean and median represent average pay levels, while the minimum and maximum show the lowest and highest reported salaries. The standard deviation and IQR show how much salaries vary within each locale. These summaries reveal that faculty pay is not equal across all institution types, which suggests that salary might be influenced by setting, size, or funding levels. This also supports why salary could be related to graduation outcomes later in the analysis.

## Data Analysis

Since my research question asks whether faculty salary is related to graduation rate, and both variables are continuous, I used a linear regression model to analyze the relationship. The response variable is graduation rate (GRAD_RATE) and the explanatory variable is average faculty salary (AVGFACSAL). The goal is to see whether colleges that pay faculty more tend to have higher graduation rates.

```{r}
#Fit linear regression model
model <- lm(GRAD_RATE ~ AVGFACSAL, data = college_clean)

#View coefficients
library(broom)
tidy(model)
```

The output shows the intercept and slope of the regression line. The slope for average faculty salary is positive, meaning graduation rate increases slightly as faculty salary increases. This means colleges with higher average salaries tend to have higher graduation rates on average.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Model summary
glance(model) %>%
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, statistic, p.value) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

The glance() output shows that the model’s R-squared is about 0.25, which means faculty salary explains around 25% of the variation in graduation rate. The p-value for salary is very small (p < 0.001), so the relationship between salary and graduation rate is statistically significant. This means we reject the idea that salary and graduation rate are unrelated, and conclude that higher faculty pay is associated with better student outcomes. However, the model is only moderately strong, so salary is not the only factor that affects graduation rates.


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Predicted values for visualization

college_clean$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = college_clean)

ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = predicted, y = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "green") +
  geom_abline(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Observed vs Predicted Graduation Rates",
    x = "Predicted Graduation Rate (%)",
    y = "Observed Graduation Rate (%)"
  )

```

This plot checks how well the model predictions match real graduation rates. Many points fall near the red line, meaning predictions follow the general trend, but the spread shows that salary does not perfectly predict graduation rate. This supports the idea that the relationship exists but is not the only influence.



```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
college_model <- college_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(GRAD_RATE), !is.na(AVGFACSAL))

college_model$predicted <- predict(model)
college_model$residuals <- resid(model)

ggplot(college_model, aes(x = predicted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs Predicted Values",
    x = "Predicted Graduation Rate (%)",
    y = "Residuals"
  )

```

This plot tests constant variance. The residuals are mostly centered around zero without a strong funnel shape, meaning variance is decently consistent. However, the spread shows that the model does not capture all influences on graduation rate. This suggests the linear model is acceptable, but not completely accurate.


```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
qqnorm(college_model$residuals)
qqline(college_model$residuals, col = "red")

```

The Q-Q plot checks normality of residuals. Most points follow the black line closely, with slight deviation at the ends. This means the normality assumption is mostly satisfied, and the model results are reliable enough for analysis.


Overall, the linear regression model suggests that colleges with higher faculty salaries tend to have higher graduation rates, and the relationship is statistically significant. However, the R-squared value shows the model explains only part of the variation, meaning other factors like funding, student preparation, or institutional resources could also play big roles. The diagnostic plots showed that assumptions for linear regression are mostly met, so the analysis is valid. Based on this, faculty salary should be viewed as one contributing factor to student success, not the only one.


## Conclusion

This project investigated whether average faculty salary is associated with a college’s graduation rate using the U.S. College Scorecard dataset. From the visualizations, both graduation rate and faculty salary showed noticeable variation across institutions, with most schools falling in the middle range for both variables. The scatter plot showcased a clear positive trend, suggesting that colleges paying higher salaries often report higher graduation rates. The scatter plot by locale also showed this pattern across different college settings, although the spread of points revealed that the relationship is not consistent everywhere. Summary statistics supported these observations by showing that both graduation rates and salary levels vary considerably between institutions, and that locale categories differ in sample size and salary distribution.

The linear regression model confirmed this pattern statistically. The salary coefficient was positive and very significant (p < 0.001), meaning it is extremely unlikely that the relationship occurred by random chance. However, the R-squared value of around 0.25 showed that average faculty salary explains only about 25% of the variation in graduation rates, inferring that other important factors are not included in this model. The diagnostic plots suggested that the model assumptions were mostly met, in that residuals were fairly scattered, and the Q-Q plot showed only minor deviations from normality. Together, these results support the conclusion that higher faculty salaries are associated with higher graduation rates, but salary should be viewed as only one contributor among many that influence student success.
